passages.title: Little Free Libraries
passages.text:
Walk down a quiet street in many towns in North America, and you might see something that looks like a large birdhouse standing on a post in someone's front garden. Look closer, and you will find that it is full of books. A small sign says: 'Take a book. Return a book.' This is a Little Free Library, and there are now more than a hundred thousand of them around the world.

The idea began in 2009 in the small town of Hudson, Wisconsin, in the United States. A man named Todd Bol wanted to remember his mother, a former teacher who had loved reading. He built a wooden box shaped like a little schoolhouse, filled it with books and put it outside his home. His neighbours loved it so much that he built more and gave them away. With a friend, Rick Brooks, he soon turned the idea into a non-profit organisation that encourages people everywhere to build their own.

The rules are simple. Anyone can open the box, borrow a book and keep it for as long as they like. There is no library card, no fee and no deadline. Many people bring back the book they took, or leave a different one for the next reader. The owners of the libraries, who are usually ordinary families, schools or cafés, look after them and add new books from time to time.

Supporters say that the little libraries do more than share books. Because people stop to look inside, neighbours who never spoke before start chatting with each other. In areas where there is no public library nearby, children can find something to read without travelling far. Some critics, however, point out that many of the boxes stand in wealthy neighbourhoods, where people already have easy access to books.

Next time you see a small box of books by the road, why not stop, choose one and leave one of your own?

sourceNote: 2022–2026 оны жишиг эх нь албан БҮТ-ийн эх биш, нийтэд нээлттэй хуулбар; 2018–2020 оны албан хувилбарын бүтцийг баримталсан.
